chunks: Hamza ibn Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Zayd ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him) in Qum in the year 339 A.H. said: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Sa'id al-Kufi, the freedman of the Banu Hashim, informed us; he said: Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad ibn Hammad informed me; he said: Ghiyath ibn Ibrahim informed us; he said: Al-Husayn ibn Zayd ibn Ali informed us, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from his forefathers, from Ali (peace be upon them).

The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Give glad tidings - three times - indeed, the similitude of my nation is like that of abundant rain, one does not know whether its beginning is good or its end. Indeed, the similitude of my nation is like a garden from which one group eats for a year, then another group eats from it for a year. Perhaps the last group will be its most powerful in sea-depth, deepest in length, and most fruitful in branches. How can a nation be destroyed which begins with me, has twelve of the prosperous and those of understanding after me, and ends with the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary? But from among that, the offspring of chaos will be destroyed; they are not from me and I am not from them.'
ai.seo_question: What are the two similes used by the Prophet to describe the Muslim nation in this hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Uyun Akhbar al-Rida* employs the metaphors of rain and a garden to illustrate the enduring vitality and diversity of the Ummah, anchored by the twelve Imams and the return of Jesus (Isa). It distinguishes the faithful 'offspring of chaos' (Najt al-Harj) from the true believers, emphasizing that the Prophet and the twelve Imams are the 'happy ones' (Sa'ada) who guarantee the community's survival against internal strife.
